# Proposal

We would like DAG to analyse the H3K9me3 CUT and TAG samples.

## Context: Manuscript in revision

Reviewers asked for:

1. We detect changes in H3K9me3 level (increase upon differentiation) by mass spectrometry. Reviewers ask to discriminate between H3K9me3 genome wide changes and site-specific changes: We did a H3K9me3 CUT & TAG +/- differentiation.
1. To uncover the role of SETDB1 in H3K9me3 deposition upon differentiation: H3K9me3 CUT & TAG +/-SETDB1 depletion.

## Experimental Design: Samples and Conditions

We are comparing two cell types and two siRNA treatments, yielding four biological conditions:

1.	iPS control
2.	iPS SETDB1 siRNA
3.	48-hour PSM differentiated control
4.	48-hour PSM differentiated SETDB1 siRNA

Each condition includes four biological replicates, so 16 samples in total.

Sequencing depth: CUT&Tag: Paired-end reads, ~8 million reads per sample
To generate the CUT and TAG DNA libraires we used the kit from [active motif](https://www.activemotif.com/catalog/1395/cut-tag-it-express).

## Drosophila spike in

We have used Drosophila melanogaster nuclei as a heterologous spike-in control that we can use as a reliable normalization strategy. Drosophila spike in is added to all cut and tag replicates. The [Active Motif product](https://www.activemotif.com/catalog/1377/cut-tag-spike-in) was used. 


## Timeline

H3K9me3 CUT and Tag samples data available NOW.
In revision for manuscript so would be good to have results in December.
Grant must be charged before end of 2025 so need an idea of working hours.

## Biological Questions

1.	Where are H3K9me3 peaks located across the genome in iPSCs and PSM cells?
2.	Differential analysis: How do these peaks change with differentiation and change with SETDB1 knockdown?
3.	Since these marks are associated with heterochromatic and repetitive regions, we want to include multi-mapping reads in the analysis to ensure comprehensive detection of repetitive sequences.
4.	What are the genes and chromatin feature close by to the peaks (within 10kB?). 
5.	Motif enrichment analysis within the peaks?
6.	Potentially: correlate ATAC-seq changes with H3K9me3 changes. Are the regions that loose accessibility the ones that gain H3K9me3?

 
Data Analysis Plan: Pipeline Overview (I have no experience so just a wild guess)
1.	Alignment: Align FASTQ reads to the human reference genome using Bowtie2.
2.	Peak Calling: Identify enriched regions using MACS2.
3.	Quantification: Generate per-sample peak counts and merge replicates.
4.	Annotation: Annotate peaks relative to genomic features (e.g., promoters, enhancers, repeats).
5.	Differential Analysis: Identify condition-specific peaks using DESeq2 or DiffBind.
6.	Visualization and Interpretation: Perform clustering, PCA, and generate genome browser tracks (e.g., IGV).

# Data analysis

The data analysis was conducted in two stages. The first stage was carried out on the Life Sciences cluster using a Snakemake script. This stage encompassed the cleaning, quality control, and mapping of FASTQ files. The software versions employed in this stage are listed in @sec-cluster-software. In the second stage, the data were imported into [Positron](https://github.com/posit-dev/positron) and further processed using R. The versions of the R packages utilized are detailed in @sec-packages. All code used in this project is available on [GitHub](https://github.com/bartongroup/MG_HippoSeq).

# Design

@tbl-metadata presents the full experimental design. The `Sample` column contains the sample names referenced throughout this report. The Pilot samples were removed from downstream analysis (see below for explanation).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-metadata
#| tbl-cap: Design of the experiment.
tar_read(metadata) |> 
  select(Experiment = experiment, Sample = sample, `Original sample` = raw_sample, `Time point` = time_point, Treatment = treatment, Group = group, Replicate = replicate) |> 
  gt_table() |> 
  cols_align(
    align = "left",
    columns = c("Sample", "Original sample", "Group")
  )
```


# Sequencing and mapping

## Sequencing

Sequencing was done by Novogene. We have received 2x150 bp paired-end reads.

## FastQ screen {#sec-fastq-screen}

[FastQ
screen](https://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastq_screen/)
was used to map a sample of reads to several genomes to check for
contamination. @fig-fscreen shows one hit one genome percentage. Note,
the fill scale is logarithmic with grey indicating zero. There is no
notable contamination from other organisms.

There is, however, a surprisingly large proportion of Drosophila hits from di-methyl samples (Me2). @tbl-fscreen shows the numbers of reads aligned to each genome. *Fastq Screen* maps 100,000 randomly selected reads to each genome. While in tri-methyl samples Drosophila receives ~1000 hits per sample, much less than a typical 40,000-50,000 human hits, in di-methyl samples Drosophila hits are often *much* larger than the human reads, and the drosophila/human ratio of the counts varies dramatically between samples.

```{r}
#| label: fig-fscreen
#| fig-cap: Fscreen results, one hit per one genome and multiple hits per one genome are inluded. The colour scale is logarithmic and grey indicates no hits.
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
tar_read(fig_fscreen)
```



```{r}
#| label: tbl-fscreen
#| tbl-cap: FastQ screen one hit per genome counts. FastQ screen samples 100,000 random reads from each FASTQ file to do the mapping.
tar_read(fscrn) |>
  filter( name == "#One_hit_one_genome") |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = Genome, names_from = sample, values_from = value) |>
  arrange(desc(Me2_iPS_Ctrl_1)) |> 
  gt_table()
```

## Read quality

@fig-read-qual shows read quality as a function of base pair position,
@fig-read-qual-clust shows hierarchical clustering based on read
quality. This has nothing to do with biology, but rather shows potential
batch effects related to sequencing, e.g. different flow cells,
different instruments. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-read-qual
#| fig-cap: Read quality.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
tar_read(fig_read_qual) 
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-read-qual-clust
#| fig-cap: Clustering based on read quality.
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 5
tar_read(fig_read_qual_clust)
```

## Mapping

```{r}
#| label: config
tar_load(config)
```

[Bowtie2](https://bowtie-bio.sourceforge.net/bowtie2/index.shtml) was used to map reads to the human GRCh38 and drosophila BDGP6.54 genomes.

Following recommendations from the [CUT&Tag tutorial](https://yezhengstat.github.io/CUTTag_tutorial/#31_Bowtie2_alignment_[required]), the parameters used for the human genome were:

```
--end-to-end --very-sensitive --no-mixed --no-discordant --phred33 -I 10 -X 700
```

for the drosophila, two additional parameters were used: `--no-overlap --no-dovetail`.


## Mapping properties

@fig-bowtie-sum shows mapping summaries. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-bowtie-sum
#| fig-cap: Mapping summaries from bowtie2 for the (A) human and (B) drosophila alignments.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
pl1 <- tar_read(fig_bowtie_sum_human)
pl2 <- tar_read(fig_bowtie_sum_dm)
plot_grid(pl1, pl2, nrow = 1, labels = c("A", "B"))
```

## Duplication levels

`picard MarkDuplicates` was used to mark and count duplicates in the BAM files.

```{r}
#| label: fig-picard-dup
#| fig-cap: Duplication levels in the human alignments.
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 5
tar_read(fig_picard_dup)
```

## Spike-in properties

@sec-fastq-screen showed a large proportion of Drosophila reads in di-methyl samples based on random 100,000 reads. @fig-spikein-ratios shows the percentage of Drosophila mapped reads in all mapped reads. Di-methyl samples contain a lot of Drosophila reads, in some cases there is more Drosophila than human. Also, the percentage of Drosophila varies a lot between replicates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-spikein-ratios
#| fig-cap: The percentage of spikein mapped reads (both single- and multi-mapping) in the total mapped reads (both drosophila and human).
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 5
tar_read(fig_spikein_ratios)
```

## Read count per chromosome

```{r}
#| label: fig-chrom-reads
#| fig-cap: Mapped read count per chromosome for each sample.
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 30
tar_read(fig_chrom_reads) 
```
